title: Is There an Accountant Shortage in 2026?
summary: Learn why the US faces an accountant shortage, what’s driving the talent gap, how it affects businesses, and potential solutions.

- Is There an Accountant Shortage in 2026?


There is a shortage of accountants in the USA, and it’s been building for a while. According to the latest[American Institute of Certified Public Accountants (AICPA) Trends Report](https://www.aicpa-cima.com/professional-insights/download/2025-trends-report) , completed accounting degrees have declined steadily since 2010, and the number of new CPA candidates has fallen from nearly 50,000 in 2010 to 28,082 in 2024.


While the accountant shortage is real and ongoing, it doesn’t affect every industry or business equally. Firms that have adopted AI tools or outsourced part of their accounting work tend to feel it less, including the[45% of middle-market companies](https://uhy-us.com/media/gbjb5xmx/middle-market-survey-2025.pdf) now using outsourced accounting resources.


Learn more about what’s driving the CPA shortage and what it means for emerging professionals and business owners.


## **Key Points**


- Demand for accountants is high. The[US Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS)](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/business-and-financial/accountants-and-auditors.htm#tab-6) projects an average of 115,300 annual openings through 2035. Many of these openings come from professionals retiring or moving into other lines of work.
- Despite a positive job outlook, 84% of senior leaders feel there’s a finance and accounting talent shortage, according to a[2026 CFO Pulse Survey](https://2399470.fs1.hubspotusercontent-na1.net/hubfs/2399470/Personiv%20Sales%20Share%20Hub%20Collateral/2026%20Survey%20Report/Spring-Summer/2026%20Personiv%20Talent%20Survey%20-%20June%20Summer.pdf) .
- Baby boomer retirements and shifting pay and work-life expectations are among the commonly cited drivers of the shortage of accountants.
- For firms, the decline in accountants affects everything from client turnover rates and staff workloads to closing cycles.
- With the accountant shortage comes new opportunities, especially for professionals drawn to advisory and tech-forward roles.


## **The Shortage by the Numbers**


From now through 2035, the[BLS](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/business-and-financial/accountants-and-auditors.htm#tab-1) projects a 5% increase in accounting employment. That’s faster than the average across all occupations and translates to about 115,300 openings each year from new positions and retirements combined.


But despite the growing need for talented professionals, firms across the board are struggling to fill those openings. Figures from the 2025 AICPA Trends Report tell the story:


- There were only 74,175 unique certified public accountant (CPA) candidates in 2024 versus 103,609 in 2010. This is almost as low as it was during the height of the COVID-19 pandemic.
- Just 13,070 CPA candidates passed the fourth and final section of the exam in 2024, down from 29,539 in 2010.
- The completion of bachelor’s degrees in accounting fell 3.3% year-over-year in 2023-2024. For master’s degrees, the completion rate dropped 15%.


Retirements are compounding the accounting talent shortage. Roughly 340,000 accountants have left the profession in the past five years, per[Fortune](https://fortune.com/article/gen-z-reviving-accounting-profession-six-figure-salaries-irs-volunteer-income-tax-assistance-program-vita/) , and more departures are expected as baby boomers continue to age out of senior roles.


## **What’s Driving the Talent Gap**


The accountant shortage is due to a combination of factors. Not only are talented professionals retiring faster than companies can replace them, but fewer students are majoring in accounting. And then there’s the growing debate about whether CPA licensure is worth the cost and effort.


### **Retirements Are Outpacing New Hires**


With the wave of accountants exiting the profession comes the challenge of replacing decades of institutional knowledge and long-nurtured client relationships. Education and a few years on the job can’t fully replace the judgment that comes with 20 or 30 years of practice.


Meanwhile, the supply of junior accountants and newly licensed CPAs is tightening, too, pushing firms to compete harder for talent just to maintain current capacity.


### **Fewer Students Are Choosing Accounting**


According to the AICPA report, US schools awarded 55,152 bachelor’s and master’s degrees in accounting in 2023-24, down from 78,137 a decade earlier. This is a 29% decline and firms reported hiring 11,985 new graduates for accounting-based roles in 2025, but only 75% of these majored in accounting.


CPA exam participation has followed a similar downward trajectory, according to the AICPA report. There were 91,363 unique CPA candidates in 2014. In 2024, that number had fallen to 74,175, nearly a 19% drop.


According to a[Center for Audit Quality (CAQ) survey of roughly 1,800 students and recent graduates](https://www.thecaq.org/pipelineresearch2023) , the top reasons students don’t choose accounting are a lack of interest or passion in the subject, higher starting salaries in competing majors like finance and consulting, and the additional credit hours required for CPA licensure.


For students or career-changers curious about building finance and tech skills,[Intuit for Education](https://www.intuit.com/solutions/education/) offers free tools and curriculum designed to make the fundamentals more accessible.


### **The CPA Licensure Debate**


You don’t need a CPA license to work as an accountant, but for those who want one, the path to[becoming a CPA](https://www.intuit.com/blog/life-at-intuit/intuit-experts/how-to-become-a-cpa/) can be a sticking point. The traditional route typically requires:


- 150 credit hours of coursework (typically a bachelor’s plus additional credits or a master’s)
- One to two years of supervised work experience
- A passing score (75+) on the 4-part[Uniform CPA Exam](https://www.intuit.com/blog/life-at-intuit/intuit-experts/cpa-exam/)
- Application and exam fees that often top $1,000


The[150-hour requirement](https://academy.intuit.com/blog/job-readiness/accounting/150-hour-rule-cpa/) has drawn scrutiny. In 2024,[MIT Sloan research](https://mitsloan.mit.edu/ideas-made-to-matter/150-hour-rule-cpa-certification-causes-a-26-drop-minority-entrants) found a 14% overall decline in new CPAs since the 150-hour rule took effect. That drop increased to 26% for minority populations.


In response, the AICPA and[National Association of State Boards of Accountancy (NASBA)](https://nasba.org/blog/2025/12/23/new-cpa-licensure-pathways-and-cpa-mobility/) have introduced an[alternative pathway to licensure](https://nasba.org/blog/2025/12/23/new-cpa-licensure-pathways-and-cpa-mobility/) that requires 120 credit hours (bachelor’s level), two years of supervised work experience, and a passing CPA Exam score.


[Many states have or plan to adopt some form of the new model](https://www.cfodive.com/news/broadening-cpa-licensure-paths-marching-beyond-150-hour-rule-accounting-talent-shortage/745282/) , giving candidates more flexibility in how they qualify and signaling a meaningful shift in how the profession is approaching the pipeline problem.


### **Pay and Work-Life Expectations Have Shifted**


According to the BLS, accountants earn a median annual wage of $83,680, though the lowest 10% earn under $56,020. More senior and licensed professionals typically earn well above the median, but for incoming candidates, the upfront time and cost of entry can be harder to justify against starting pay.


Work-life expectations have also evolved. Accountants generally keep to a standard 40-hour week, but busy periods like tax season often require significant overtime.


Comparable roles in tech and finance may offer stronger starting compensation with similar or lower educational barriers. Financial analysts, for example, work full time and earn a median annual wage of[$103,570](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/business-and-financial/financial-analysts.htm) , with a bachelor’s degree as the typical entry point (though many pursue additional certifications to advance).


## **Business and Industry Impacts**


Between 81% and 95% of companies report experiencing an accounting talent shortage, according to the 2026 CFO Pulse Survey. The number varies depending on the size of the organization, with larger companies hit hardest by the lack of qualified professionals.


### **Public Accounting Firms**


For public accounting firms, the accounting shortage can show up across operations:


- **Staff overload:** Fewer accountants means an increased workload for everyone else. That can quickly lead to burnout or higher employee turnover rates.
- **Greater error risk:** As accountants struggle to keep up, the risk of financial errors or other inaccuracies rises, especially with compressed timelines. Compliance missteps might also follow.
- **Higher client turnover:** Clients put a lot of trust in accounting professionals to correctly handle their taxes and other financials. With fewer accountants comes the possibility of delayed reporting and other mistakes that threaten that trust.


Rising compensation costs are another concern as firms need to find ways to attract (and retain) talent. In the CFO Pulse Survey, 51% of finance leaders agreed that rising salary expectations are their No. 1 hiring challenge right now.


### **Corporate Finance Departments**


Firms rely on accountants to do more than process invoices or close the books. Today’s CPAs are often expected to take on higher-value work, like:


- Auditing (internal, external)
- Financial reporting
- Strategic advisement/consulting
- Business growth strategies


With fewer qualified accountants, the capacity for this kind of work diminishes. For in-house teams, the shortage means:


- Longer close cycles
- Audit friction due to delayed reporting
- Greater risk of reporting errors and missed deadlines
- Consolidated responsibilities due to more demanding workloads


The accounting talent shortage also means multi-month hiring gaps from even short-term departures. For 50% of large companies (5,000+ employees), the CFO Pulse Survey found it takes an average of 120 days to fill open finance and accounting roles. That’s time lost on driving value for businesses and clients.


### **Small Businesses and Individual Taxpayers**


The ripple effect of the shortage of accountants reaches well beyond the firms themselves.


When qualified accountants are harder to find or too expensive to hire, small business owners might end up managing their own books. And that raises the risk of delayed or inaccurate tax filings, which could result in fines or other penalties. In some cases, errors can be significant enough to trigger an audit.


For individual taxpayers who can’t afford the rising service costs, it’s also harder to get timely tax help. Over- or underpayment is a real possibility for those doing their taxes themselves. There’s also an increased risk of missed deadlines or audits.


Filing taxes well without a CPA is possible, though, and the tools and training to do it are more accessible than ever. For those interested in building that skill, learn[how to become a tax preparer](https://www.intuit.com/blog/life-at-intuit/intuit-experts/how-to-become-a-tax-preparer/) .


### **Geographic Variation**


While there is a shortage of accountants in the USA overall, the pressure hits some firms harder than others.


Firms in smaller or more rural areas might feel the accounting shortage most acutely, but it eases somewhat at larger firms. That might be due to bigger budgets for technology or process automation.


In the CFO Pulse Survey, 26% of firms that have invested in AI and automation report efficiency and productivity gains. That’s up from just 23% a year earlier, and nearly every respondent reported some form of AI or automation already in use.


Region matters, too. According to[Intuit’s State of Accounting Jobs report](https://www.intuit.com/blog/innovative-thinking/accountant-job-outlook-demand-report/) , competition for qualified accountants is highest in big cities, like:


- Atlanta (GA)
- Dallas-Fort Worth (TX)
- Nashville (TN)
- Charlotte (NC)
- Greater Hartford (CT)


In these metropolitan areas, firms face year-round hiring pressure. Accountants with more specialized experience are particularly sought after, which means greater competition within a relatively limited candidate pool.


## **How Organizations Can Respond**


The accountant shortage is a challenge, but firms can get ahead of it by combining strategic recruitment, tech solutions, and internal programs to attract and retain talent.


### **Recruiting and Retention Strategies**


As per the 2026 CFO Pulse Survey, 43% of finance leaders say senior accountant is the hardest role to fill. Staff accountant (26%) and tax accountant (11%) are next on the list.


With fewer skilled professionals and shifting expectations, companies can better compete for talent by:


- Introducing higher market-rate salaries
- Allowing for more flexible scheduling
- Providing on-the-job mentorship opportunities
- Offering clearer career advancement paths
- Hiring from adjacent fields, like business or finance


### **Technology and AI in Accounting**


Roughly[76% of financial services businesses](https://kpmg.com/us/en/articles/2024/ai-in-finance-us-report.html) have made progress piloting or using AI for accounting, second only to financial planning (78%). Adoption tends to concentrate in high-volume, rules-based work, including:


- Transaction categorization
- Expense tracking
- Data entry
- Receipt matching
- Account reconciliations


Technology can help ease the strain, but it isn’t a full answer on its own. As the profession shifts toward advisory work and exception handling, human judgment stays central for navigating regulatory gray areas and sustaining client relationships.


### **Expanding the Talent Pipeline**


The alternative pathway to becoming a CPA is encouraging for those considering an accounting career. Firms can go further by widening the entry points themselves:


- **Internships/apprenticeships** :[Three in five students](https://www.journalofaccountancy.com/issues/2026/aug/how-to-set-up-an-effective-internship-program/) who intern at a company end up getting a job offer, which most end up accepting.
- **Reskilling or on-the-job training programs** : According to[DeVry University](https://www.devry.edu/content/dam/devry_edu/newsroom/2024-devry-ai-report.pdf) , almost 9 in 10 companies offer paid upskilling benefits, though only about half of employees take advantage of them.
- **Alternative credentials** :[DeVry also finds that 67% of employees](https://www.devry.edu/content/dam/devry_edu/newsroom/2024-devry-ai-report.pdf) are open to lifelong learning or alternative credentials that help them advance in their careers.
- **Employer-sponsored tuition** : Just[57% of employers](https://www.ifebp.org/resources---news/news-and-regulatory-updates/press-room/press-releases/2024/12/18/student-loan-repayment-benefits-on-the-rise) offer tuition assistance or reimbursement, which could be a deterrent given education costs for accountants.


For free accounting and financial education resources, explore Intuit’s[Accounting Futures program](https://www.intuit.com/solutions/education/accounting-futures/) .


## **The Future of the Accounting Profession**


The accounting industry is changing quickly, shaped by evolving expectations and technology. Here’s where roles are headed and what firms are doing to make the profession more accessible.


### **How Accounting Roles Are Evolving**


As AI and automation take over more of the routine work, accountants are moving toward higher-value functions, including:


- Financial analysis
- Advisory services
- Technology oversight
- Strategic decision support


Employers are placing greater value on data fluency, business judgment, and communication. The ability to thrive under pressure and make smart decisions without losing empathy are vital to success.


### **Making the Profession More Accessible**


A high barrier to entry has long contributed to the accounting shortage, and while the pipeline won’t refill overnight, several changes are already lowering the bar:


- Introduction of the new 120-credit-hour pathway to CPA licensure, now offered alongside the traditional route in many states
- Scholarships for students majoring in areas like finance or accounting
- Employer-sponsored CPA Exam support or tuition reimbursement
- Non-traditional education providers and online learning platforms like Intuit for Education


### **Practical Next Steps**


For aspiring accountants, the shortage creates real leverage. That means it could be a good time to launch your career or pursue the CPA license you’ve been putting off.


However, job opportunities and demand are uneven across businesses. Many large firms are already finding ways to make up for the shortage by using automation and AI-powered solutions. And some have combined these solutions with in-house teams and outsourced accounting to cover talent gaps and intermediate-level work.


Smaller and mid-sized firms may have less tech infrastructure in place, which can make it easier to break in but may come with lower starting pay or fewer benefits.


When weighing roles, look past the starting salary. Career advancement, mentorship, CPA Exam support, and tuition reimbursement could matter more in the long run.


## **FAQs**


###


The shortage of accountants used to be associated with public firms, particularly during busy tax season. Now, it’s a year-round issue for firms of all sizes. According to a[Controllers Council report](https://controllerscouncil.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/2026-Corporate-Finance-Accounting-Talent-Study-626.pdf) , 61% of corporate finance and accounting organizations are struggling to keep their accounting departments fully staffed.


###


Small towns and rural areas do tend to struggle the most with the accounting talent shortage. That’s largely because qualified professionals tend to move to larger cities where pay is higher, and opportunities are more abundant.


###


Yes, internationally trained accountants could help with the talent shortage. According to a[2025 AICPA report](https://www.incpas.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/2025-national-map-survey-executive-summary.pdf) , 29% of firms outsource at least some of their accounting needs to offshore workers.
